meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I've found that you don't need to wear a necktie if you can hit'?
meta.ogDescription: Widely credited to Ted Williams, but no primary source. Oldest printing located is Lee Allen's The American League Story (1962), dated April 1940.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox left fielder; the last man to bat .400
answer.sourceLine: The line is credited to Williams everywhere and to nobody else, and it fits a man who spent sixty years refusing to put a tie on. But no primary source has been found. The oldest printing we could locate is a chapter epigraph in Lee Allen’s The American League Story (1962), where it is credited “TED WILLIAMS, APRIL 1940” with no newspaper, interview or book named behind the date — and the sentence is absent from the digitised volumes searched, including Williams’s own My Turn at Bat.

source.excerpt: I’ve found that you don’t need to wear a necktie if you can hit. —TED WILLIAMS, APRIL 1940
trail: Quote Investigator has never taken this line up, and the English Wikiquote page for Ted Williams ↗ does not carry it at all — not among its quotations, not flagged as doubtful. The one misquotation specialist who touches it at all is Ralph Keyes, whose “Nice Guys Finish Seventh” (1992) discusses the sentence’s wording — its full-text snippet runs “…words were, ‘You don’t have to wear a necktie if you can hit.’ I like Buck’s version better” — but that scan is lending-restricted, and whether Keyes also rules on the attribution is a page we could not read.

An exact-phrase sweep of the Internet Archive’s digitised books finds twenty-one volumes containing the phrase ↗. The oldest is from 1962; the next oldest is Kevin Nelson’s Baseball’s Greatest Quotes, published in 1982.

That 1962 printing is Lee Allen’s The American League Story ↗ (Hill and Wang), where the sentence opens a chapter as an epigraph credited “TED WILLIAMS, APRIL 1940.” Allen was a respected baseball historian, but he names no periodical, and the book carries no note for it.

Williams’s dislike of neckwear is real and thoroughly documented — SABR’s “Ties in Baseball (and Beyond)” ↗ follows it from the 1948 Red Sox dress code to a 1991 White House ceremony — but that article never quotes this sentence.
source.excerptNote: This is how the sentence stands at the head of a chapter in Lee Allen’s 1962 history; the chapter’s first words are “When Ted Williams was a little boy…” Allen supplies the April 1940 date himself and cites nothing behind it, which is why this page stops at “attributed.”

source.rightsNote: Uncertain, and deliberately so. No publication has been tied to this wording, so there is no work whose copyright status can be assessed — and the earliest printing we did find, Lee Allen’s The American League Story (Hill and Wang, 1962), is comfortably inside copyright itself. If the remark really was made in April 1940 it would first have appeared in a newspaper or magazine, and that item has not been identified. Treat the line as unclear-rights; do not assume it is public domain.

author.name: Ted Williams
author.heading: Who was Ted Williams?
author.metaLine: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox left fielder · last .400 hitter in the major leagues
author.bio: Theodore Samuel Williams was born in San Diego in 1918 and spent his entire major-league career with the Boston Red Sox, 1939–1942 and 1946–1960, losing most of five seasons to service as a Marine Corps aviator in the Second World War and Korea. He hit .406 in 1941 — no one has hit .400 since — finished with a .344 average and 521 home runs, won two Triple Crowns and two MVP awards, and was elected to the Hall of Fame on the first ballot in 1966. He was also famously, permanently informal about neckwear: he first refused a Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1991 rather than wear a tuxedo, and when the White House relented to a necktie he turned up without one anyway and had it knotted for him by his lawyer.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: Nobody has ever credited this line to anyone but Ted Williams, so there is no rival claimant to expose. The problems are quieter: no source anywhere behind it, and a wording that has been trimmed and re-punctuated on its way through forty years of quotation books.

items.who: “I found you don’t have to wear a necktie if you can hit”
items.why: John A. Mercurio’s Chronology of Boston Red Sox Records (Harper and Row, 1989) prints it in this form, and Charles C. Alexander’s Breaking the Slump (Columbia University Press, 2002) as “you don’t have to wear a necktie — if you can hit.” Both drifts are visible in the Internet Archive full-text results ↗.

items.who: “You don’t need to wear a necktie if you can hit”
items.why: The opening “I’ve found that” is the first thing to go. Kathryn Petras’s Dance First, Think Later reduces it to a bare maxim as rule no. 528. Ralph Keyes’s misquotation reference “Nice Guys Finish Seventh” (HarperCollins, 1992) drifts on both axes at once — it drops the opening and switches need to have, printing “You don’t have to wear a necktie if you can hit” — so it belongs to the row above as much as to this one. Both are visible in the same full-text sweep ↗.

items.who: My Turn at Bat or The Science of Hitting
items.why: Quote pages sometimes imply the line comes from Williams’s own writing. Neither of his books is among the twenty-one digitised volumes that contain the phrase ↗.

The famous Red Sox necktie moment belongs to the manager, not the hitter: with everyone wondering how his new coat-and-tie rule would apply to Williams, McCarthy settled it wordlessly — greeting his star at spring training in Sarasota in an open collar, as SABR recounts from Ben Bradlee Jr.’s biography ↗. That is a story about Williams, not a sentence from him, and it is 1948 — eight years after the date Allen attaches to this quotation.

misattribution.truthLine: The credit is not in dispute; the paperwork is. The oldest printing anyone can point to is Lee Allen’s 1962 history ↗, and Allen’s own “April 1940” is an assertion rather than a citation.

context.heading: Why the tie mattered
lead: Williams’s war with neckwear is one of the best-documented things about him. When President George H. W. Bush offered him the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1991 he declined outright rather than get into a tuxedo; the White House sent word that a necktie would do; and he arrived on the day in gray slacks and a powder-blue shirt, still saying “I’m not wearing a tie,” until his lawyer knotted one for him. The Society for American Baseball Research collects the whole run of it, sourced to Ben Bradlee Jr.’s The Kid.

So the sentiment is unimpeachable. What is missing is the moment. Somebody, at some point, boiled Williams’s attitude into a single line, and by 1962 it was good enough to head a chapter of a serious American League history. Whether Williams said it in April 1940 in those words, or a sportswriter tidied it into that shape afterwards, is the part no source we could reach will settle.
detailsBody: An exact-phrase full-text sweep of the Internet Archive’s digitised books returns twenty-one volumes carrying “necktie if you can hit.” The oldest is Lee Allen’s 1962 history; the next oldest is Kevin Nelson’s Baseball’s Greatest Quotes (Simon and Schuster, 1982), and almost everything after that is a quotation or trivia compilation.

That corpus is books, not newspapers — which is exactly where an April 1940 remark would have been printed first. Library of Congress, HathiTrust and Google Books full-text searches were all refused or rate-limited during this check, so the newspaper record remains open. If a period clipping turns up, this page moves to “verified.” Until then, “attributed” is the honest label.
context.pull: The tie story is true. The sentence is the part nobody can source.

sourcesVerified.claim: An exact-phrase search for "necktie if you can hit" across Internet Archive digitised books returns 21 volumes; the oldest is Lee Allen's The American League Story (1962), whose OCR snippet reads "...need to wear a necktie if you can hit. —TED WILLIAMS, APRIL 1940 / WHEN Ted Williams was a little boy..."; variants appear in Mercurio (1989), Keyes (1992), Alexander (2002) and Petras; neither of Williams's own books is among the results.
Lee Allen, The American League Story, published by Hill & Wang, New York, 1962, 298 pages — the volume containing the earliest located printing of the line.
A second Internet Archive scan of the same title confirms the author, publisher and 1962 publication date, and its OCR carries the same epigraph and dateline.

Wikiquote's Ted Williams article contains only 'Quotes' and 'Quotes about Ted Williams' sections and does not include the necktie line in any section — there is no Sourced, Disputed or Misattributed ruling on it.

SABR's 'Ties in Baseball (and Beyond)' documents Williams's lifelong aversion to neckties, Joe McCarthy's 1948 spring-training open-collar gesture (citing Ben Bradlee Jr., The Kid, p. 295), and the 1991 Medal of Freedom episode in which Williams insisted 'I'm not wearing a tie' — but it does not quote the line under investigation.

Ted Williams was born 30 August 1918 and died 5 July 2002; he played for the Boston Red Sox 1939–1942 and 1946–1960, batted .406 in 1941, finished at .344 with 521 home runs, won two Triple Crowns and two AL MVP awards, and was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1966; his books are My Turn at Bat (1969) and The Science of Hitting (1970).

Ralph Keyes, "Nice guys finish seventh": false phrases, spurious sayings, and familiar misquotations, HarperCollins, New York, 1992 — bibliographic record for the misquotation reference that carries a shortened form of the line.
